n: This is the only place the Bible names the temple site “mount Moriah.” It ties together Abraham’s near-sacrifice of Isaac and the spot where God stopped the plague in David’s day — a place of substitution and mercy that points to Christ.

f.w: the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite
f.g: Ornan is called Araunah in Samuel.

n: Construction began in the second month of Solomon’s fourth year, about 966 BC — a date remembered as a turning point in Israel’s history.

f.w: the fourth year of his reign

n: The main building was 60 cubits long and 20 wide (about 90 by 30 feet). The “first measure” refers to the older, longer cubit.

f.g: The older royal cubit, about 20.6 inches (52 cm), slightly longer than the common cubit.
A cubit was the length from elbow to fingertip, roughly 18 inches (45 cm).

n: The front porch was 20 cubits wide. Its listed height of 120 cubits is surprisingly tall; some ancient manuscripts read 20, which fits better. Its interior was gold-covered.

f.g: Some Greek and Syriac texts read ‘twenty cubits’; the figure may reflect a copying difference.

n: The main hall (the holy place) was paneled with cypress, covered with fine gold, and decorated with palm trees and chain designs — images recalling the garden of Eden and the tree of life.

f.g: Symbols of life, victory, and paradise.

n: Precious stones adorned the house, and the gold came from Parvaim, a place famous for fine gold but whose location is now unknown.

f.g: An unidentified gold-producing region, perhaps in Arabia.

n: Beams, door frames, walls, and doors were all covered in gold, and cherubim were engraved on the walls — heavenly guardians of God’s presence, like those guarding Eden.

f.g: Angelic beings who guard sacred space. (The Hebrew plural is already ‘cherubim’; KJV adds an extra -s.)

n: The most holy place was a perfect cube, 20 cubits each way, covered with 600 talents of fine gold. It was the most sacred room on earth to Israel, where God’s presence dwelt.

f.g: The holy of holies, entered only by the high priest once a year on the Day of Atonement.

n: Even the nails were gold-plated, weighing fifty shekels, and the upper rooms were also overlaid with gold.
Inside the most holy place stood two large carved cherubim, covered with gold, overshadowing the ark.
The cherubim’s wings stretched a total of twenty cubits. One cherub’s outer wing touched the wall while its inner wing touched the other cherub’s wing.
The second cherub mirrored the first: one wing to the opposite wall, the other meeting its partner’s wing in the middle — together spanning the whole room.
The two cherubim stood upright and faced inward toward the main hall, their outspread wings forming a canopy over the ark — the throne of God.

f.g: Literally ‘toward the house,’ i.e. facing the main hall.

n: A veil of blue, purple, crimson, and fine linen embroidered with cherubim separated the holy place from the most holy place. When Jesus died, the temple veil was torn — opening the way into God’s presence.
Two huge bronze pillars stood before the temple, with decorated capitals on top. (1 Kings gives each pillar’s height as 18 cubits; the 35 here may be their combined length.)

f.g: Capital — the decorated top of a column.

n: The pillar tops were decorated with chainwork and a hundred pomegranates — symbols of fruitfulness also embroidered on the high priest’s robe.

f.g: ‘Oracle’ (Hebrew devir) usually means the inner sanctuary; here the text may mean ‘like a necklace.’

n: The pillars were named Jachin (“He will establish”) and Boaz (“In Him is strength”). Their names proclaimed that God would make His house and His people firm and strong.

f.g: Hebrew ‘in Him is strength’ — also the name of David’s ancestor.
